name: PT Royaltama Mulia Kontraktorindo Tbk

frontmatter.title: Royaltama Mulia Kontraktorindo: the turnaround is real, the price already has it
frontmatter.summary: RMKO has swung from a large loss to a small nine-month profit on a surge in revenue, but the profit is a tax benefit and almost all of the revenue comes from the controlling shareholder's own group. At our through-cycle NAV the shares are worth Rp139 against Rp157, a -11.4% return: REDUCE.
thesis: The operating recovery is genuine: nine-month revenue rose 57.4% and EBITDA of IDR59.4bn is a 17.2% margin, from negative a year earlier [S2, S7].
But the reported profit is an accounting artefact: an income tax benefit of IDR6.3bn on a negative pre-tax result, not operating earnings [S7].
The customer base is the group: 94.1% of nine-month revenue is related-party, and one affiliate alone is IDR251.2bn [S7].
The fleet eats the cash: restated D&A of 70.6 IDR bn in FY2025 is more than a sixth of revenue, so capex must run near depreciation for the business to stand still [S6].
The nine-month profit is one quarter: the H1 filing shows a IDR-47.4bn net loss and Q3 alone earned IDR48.6bn, so the run-rate is not a full-year margin [S10, S9].
REDUCE at Rp139 against Rp157: the base DCF is Rp126, and the contractor peer multiple adds Rp114 rather than rescuing it, so the target is set by the base, not the tail [S0].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether Q4 repeats the Q3 margin and whether the tax benefit reverses
Commissioning of the second loading system, which doubles operated train-loading capacity
Chip-seal hauling-road completion and the volume it connects

blocks.text: **REDUCE**, twelve-month value Rp139 against a Rp157 price, a -11.4% return. The variant view is that the market has already priced the recovery: the base DCF is Rp126 and the contractor peer multiple, weighted alongside it, is Rp114, so both methods sit below the price and the target no longer depends on the bull case. The recovery's quality is also weaker than the headline.

The company is a coal mining contractor and logistics operator in South Sumatra, not a coal producer: it removes overburden, hauls coal along a 38 km dedicated road, operates the group's stockpile and train-loading station, rents heavy equipment and builds mining infrastructure [S8]. Nine months into 2026 revenue reached IDR345.3bn, up 57.4%, and EBITDA IDR59.4bn at a 17.2% margin, against negative EBITDA a year earlier [S2, S7]. That is a real operating swing, driven by construction work for the group, more third-party mines on the hauling road and train-loading volumes that more than doubled [S2]. The nine months hide the shape. The H1 filing shows a net loss of IDR-47.4bn and a gross loss of IDR-38.7bn on IDR181.2bn of revenue; Q3 alone then earned IDR48.6bn of net profit and IDR74.8bn of EBITDA [S10, S7, S9]. The quarter reconciles exactly: nine-month net profit of IDR1.2bn less the H1 loss gives the Q3 number [S7, S10]. That is a construction catch-up, not a run-rate.

Three things stop us from paying for it. First, the profit is not operating profit: the nine-month result of IDR1.2bn rests on an income tax benefit of IDR6.3bn against a pre-tax result of IDR-5.1bn [S7]. Second, the customer is the group: 94.1% of nine-month revenue is related-party, with PT Royaltama Mulia Kencana alone at IDR251.2bn [S7]. Third, the asset base is heavy and short-lived — restated D&A of 70.6 IDR bn in FY2025 [S6] means the fleet must be replaced every six years or so, so the free cash flow that survives a normal capex cycle is a fraction of EBITDA.

What moves the value: the gross margin (each point of gross margin is worth one per cent of revenue in EBIT), the capex ratio (we model 14.5% of revenue, in line with depreciation), and whether the related-party construction work continues at the 2026 pace. The reverse DCF says the current price needs 13.4% revenue growth in FY2027E to be right.

RMKO provides four things to coal mines in South Sumatra: mining services (overburden removal, coal getting, mine infrastructure), coal hauling, train loading and stockpile operation, and heavy-equipment rental, with a construction arm that builds the group's mining infrastructure [S8, S6]. FY2025 revenue split into construction services IDR157.9bn, mining services IDR126.2bn and heavy-equipment rental IDR123.5bn [S6]. The mix has moved sharply: construction was IDR22.3bn in FY2024 and is now the largest segment, at 41.6% of nine-month revenue in 2026 against IDR102.8bn of mining services and IDR98.8bn of rental [S6, S2]. That construction line is largely the group's own capital spending passing through RMKO's profit and loss; it grew because the group is building support facilities in South Sumatra, not because RMKO won open-market work [S2]. The distinction matters for how durable the revenue is.

The physical footprint is the moat and the constraint. RMKO operates a 38 km dedicated coal hauling road owned by PT RMK Energy Tbk, connecting six new mines since the first quarter of 2025 to the group's loading station; it operates the stockpile (160,000 tonnes today, 300,000 once the second loading system is running) and the train-loading system, whose capacity is 4-5 Mt a year today and 8-10 Mt after the second system starts at the end of 2027 [S8]. It owns the operating fleet: three large excavators, sixteen large haulers, 238 dump trucks, 36 small excavators, 28 dozers and support equipment [S8]. Volume follows the road rather than the coal price: hauling volume in the nine months was 1.1 Mt and train loading 2.3 Mt, both roughly double the prior year [S2]. Annualised, that train-loading figure is between three-fifths and four-fifths of the first station's capacity, so the headroom behind the forecast is real but not open-ended [S2, S8].

The company is a challenger, not a leader: it is small next to the listed contractors and its position depends on being the operator of assets owned by PT RMK Energy Tbk rather than on assets it owns itself [S8]. That is the central structural fact of the equity. RMKO listed in July 2023 at Rp450 a share [S6]; the controlling shareholder is PT RMK Investama, at 80.0% before the 2026 rights issue and 73.1% after it, with the public at 26.9% [S6, S8]. Two wholly owned subsidiaries, ROKT in construction and RMBE in concrete, sit underneath, and the company employs 992 people [S8, S6].

The economics are a fee per unit of work: overburden removed, tonnes hauled, tonnes loaded, equipment rented by the month. Rates are contractual, with fuel adjustment clauses that lag spot prices, so a rise in diesel hits margin before it is recovered in price [S7, S6]. Utilisation therefore drives profit: the same fleet on the same road earns more when more mines feed it, which is why the six third-party mines added since 2025 and the doubling of train-loading volume matter more to this equity than the coal price itself [S2, S8]. It also explains the shape of the 2025 loss: the fleet was built before the volume arrived, and depreciation ran ahead of the work it was bought for [S6].

Indonesian thermal coal output is broadly flat and the reference price has come off: HBA was 121.15 USD/t in the first period of May 2025 and 99.87 USD/t in the first period of April 2026 [S6]. The company's own read is that volume prospects remain open but prices are in a more normal and more volatile range than the 2022 peak [S6]. For a contractor the coal price matters through two channels — whether clients keep producing, and whether they keep spending on infrastructure — and both are weaker at today's reference price than at last year's. Royalty and DMO rules apply to the producers RMKO serves, not to RMKO's own profit and loss, so contractor revenue is a function of tonnage moved rather than of the price at which that tonnage is sold [S6]. That is the structural advantage of the model, and the structural disadvantage is that the contractor owns none of the resource that generates the tonnage.

The addressable market is the South Sumatra hauling and loading corridor, and the volume is captive to the road. RMKO's competitive position rests on four things it names itself: the 38 km road, the train-loading system, a partnership with PT Kereta Api Indonesia for rail capacity, and the affiliation with PT RMK Energy Tbk that gives it captive volume [S8]. Six new mines have connected to the road since the first quarter of 2025 and the company is extending access to potential mines [S8]. The moat is real but it is a group moat, not a company one: the road and the loading station belong to RMKE, and RMKO is the operator [S8]. That arrangement delivers utilisation without the capital cost of the infrastructure, which is why returns on the operating business can look good; it also means the terms are set inside the group rather than in a market, and no arm's-length rate is disclosed.

The structural reason the road matters is regulatory. A South Sumatra governor's instruction that took effect at the start of 2026 bans coal transport on public roads; the company's own deck calls the dedicated road "the exclusive logistics solution for affected mines in the region" and "the sole viable transport route" [S8 p13]. That converts the road from a convenience into a captive corridor for the mines it touches, and it is the single strongest external support for the volume growth in our forecast — support the base case does not separately capitalise and the bull case does [S8].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: fuel is the largest single cost at IDR94.5bn of IDR325.9bn of nine-month cost of revenue, and the equipment dealers have pricing power over a fleet of 238 dump trucks that has to be kept running [S7, S8]. Buyer power is high and concentrated: related parties were 94.1% of nine-month revenue and the largest customer alone IDR251.2bn, so the customer and the owner of the road sit inside the same economic family [S7]. New entrants are constrained by the road and the rail slot rather than by capital: a hauling contract is easy to bid for and hard to perform without a dedicated road and a loading slot. Substitutes are road hauling by others, which is more expensive per tonne over a route that long, and barging, which the geography makes less attractive [S8]. Rivalry is moderate among South Sumatra contractors, but the group relationship removes RMKO from open competition for its core volume.

Coal contractors in Indonesia are typically paid a rate per cubic metre of overburden removed or per tonne hauled, with fuel adjustment clauses that lag spot prices. Utilisation, not price, drives margins, which is why the number of mines connected to a dedicated road matters more than the coal price itself.

Revenue went from 272.4 IDR bn in FY2023 to 249.1 IDR bn and then 407.6 IDR bn in FY2025, but the FY2025 increase was bought: cost of revenue rose to 437.0 IDR bn and the gross result was -29.4 IDR bn [S6]. The cause is visible in the cost lines: fuel, direct materials, salaries, repairs and the restated depreciation all rose faster than revenue as construction work scaled, and construction is close to a pass-through business in which the group's capital spending appears in RMKO's revenue and in its cost base at almost the same size [S6]. The segment disclosure makes the same point from the other side: construction was IDR157.9bn of FY2025 revenue against IDR22.3bn a year earlier [S6].

The restatement that matters is depreciation. The data pack carries D&A of a few hundred million rupiah for FY2025 because the LK uses the direct cash-flow method and only the G&A depreciation line reaches the pack; the notes show the cost-of-revenue depreciation line, the right-of-use charge and the G&A line, a total of 70.6 IDR bn [S6, F10]. On that basis FY2025 EBITDA was 16.4 IDR bn, not the negative figure the pack implies, and the FY2024 figure was 52.5 IDR bn [S6]. Every margin in this report uses the restated charge.

The FY2023 comparison is not like-for-like. FY2023's 56.6 IDR bn gross profit on 272.4 IDR bn of revenue was earned while the fleet built that year (123.7 IDR bn of capex) carried almost no depreciation; the following year's 55.2 IDR bn D&A charge landed on a smaller revenue base and cut the gross result to 13.8 IDR bn [S6 p8, S0]. Construction, now 41.6% of revenue, is also a near-pass-through business with little gross margin [S2, S6]. The terminal 9.0% gross margin in the model is therefore not a claim that the business is structurally worse than it was in 2023: it is a claim that the fleet now carries its depreciation and the mix is lower-margin. A return toward the 2023 margin is the bull case, not the base.

Nine months of 2026 changed the picture. Revenue of IDR345.3bn produced a gross profit of IDR19.4bn, G&A of IDR19.1bn and an operating profit of only IDR0.3bn; D&A of IDR59.2bn is what turns that into EBITDA of IDR59.4bn [S7, S2]. The construction segment supplied IDR143.7bn of revenue, 41.6% of the total, and rental IDR98.8bn, so the growth is concentrated in the two least capital-intensive lines rather than in the mining services that carry the fleet [S2]. Below the operating line, finance costs fell to IDR4.5bn as debt was repaid, and the pre-tax result was IDR-5.1bn; the IDR6.3bn tax benefit then produced the IDR1.2bn net profit [S7]. We treat the tax benefit as non-recurring: it is a deferred-tax movement against a deferred-tax asset, not cash.

The quarter, not the nine months, is where the earnings are, and the arithmetic now ties exactly. The nine-month LK reports revenue of IDR345.3bn, gross profit of IDR19.4bn and net profit of IDR1.2bn; the H1 filing reports revenue of IDR181.2bn, a gross loss of IDR-38.7bn and a net loss of IDR-47.4bn [S7, S10]. Subtracting the H1 column from the nine-month column gives Q3 revenue of IDR164.1bn, the same number the deck and the press report, and Q3 net profit of IDR48.6bn with EBITDA of IDR74.8bn at a 45.6% margin [S7, S10, S2, S9]. The same subtraction shows that the quarter earned more gross profit than the whole nine months combined, so the first half's gross margin was deeply negative: this is a construction-revenue catch-up sitting on top of a loss-making first half, not a smooth recovery or a run-rate [S7, S10]. The company's own FY2026 target confirms the shape — full-year net profit of IDR4.3bn against IDR1.2bn earned in nine months leaves only a small Q4 residual, and full-year gross profit of IDR35.6bn against the IDR19.4bn already booked implies a Q4 gross margin far below Q3's [S8 p17]. We model Q4 at the target-implied revenue and margin, not at Q3's, which is why FY2026E EBITDA of 90.7 IDR bn sits below a simple extrapolation of the third quarter.

Our forecast has revenue at 553.1 IDR bn for FY2026E, which is the nine months actually booked plus the Q4 residual of the company's current 2026 revenue target of IDR553.1bn [S8, S7]. The old RKAP of IDR627.8bn is stale; the deck's target is the live plan and it implies a Q4 above Q4-2025, which is the seasonal pattern we use. Gross margin recovers from 6.4% to 9.0% as hauling and train loading — the higher-utilisation, higher-margin work — take a larger share [S2, S8]. EBITDA reaches 90.7 IDR bn and 117.1 IDR bn, but EBIT is only 6.9 IDR bn and 23.4 IDR bn, because depreciation of 83.8 IDR bn sits between them.

Cash flow is where the story is decided. Operating cash flow was IDR28.4bn for nine months against capex of IDR34.3bn [S7]. Working capital is negative and large — unearned revenue of IDR100.3bn, up from IDR61.3bn at the start of the year, and trade payables in excess of current assets — so growth releases cash rather than absorbing it [S7]. We model working capital at -32.0% of revenue, the ratio the September balance sheet actually shows. Against that, capex must be modelled at replacement level: the nine-month spend of IDR34.3bn is below the restated D&A charge, the fleet is depreciated over short lives, and the FY2023 build cost 123.7 IDR bn before the current volume arrived [S7, S6, S0]. We therefore use 14.5% of revenue, in line with the depreciation ratio rather than the nine-month trough, which is why free cash flow to the firm is 14.8 IDR bn in FY2026E and 31.2 IDR bn in FY2028E rather than the much larger numbers a low-capex model would show.

The balance sheet is much stronger than a year ago. The July 2026 rights issue put IDR111.7bn of cash on the balance sheet from new shares at Rp350 each, taking the share count to 1,576.7m; the controlling shareholder's stake fell from 80.0% to 73.1%, which implies it took just under half of the new shares while the public took the rest [S8, S7]. Financial debt fell to IDR56.7bn from IDR95.5bn, cash rose to IDR50.8bn, equity to IDR291.1bn and the debt-to-equity ratio to 0.19 times against a covenant ceiling of 2.5x [S2, S7]. Net debt is therefore almost nil — debt of IDR56.7bn against cash of IDR50.8bn — and the shares trade at 3.1x EV/EBITDA on our FY2026E number [S0].

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. **Accruals and cash conversion**: nine-month net profit of IDR1.2bn against operating cash flow of IDR28.4bn is not an accruals problem, but the profit itself is a tax item, which is worse — the operating result is a rounding error. **Related-party gravity**: 94.1% of revenue is related-party, up from 84.1% a year earlier, and related-party trade payables are 25.3% of trade payables and IDR82.3bn in absolute terms [S7]. This is the modal value-destruction channel on IDX and it is at the extreme here. **Divergence**: unearned revenue rose from IDR61.3bn to IDR100.3bn in nine months while revenue rose 57.4% — advances are being collected ahead of work, which flatters operating cash flow [S7]. **Structure**: a rights issue at Rp350 in July 2026 when the shares now trade at Rp157 is a per-share value leak for anyone who did not subscribe; the controlling shareholder subscribed just under half and the public the remainder [S8]. **Leverage policy**: the FY2025 debt-to-equity ratio of 2.13 times breached the company's own two-times policy ceiling before the rights issue repaired the balance sheet [S6 p8]. **IDX regime**: no special-monitoring board or notation flag was found in the filings or the press we searched [S6, S7]. **Audit**: the FY2025 opinion is unqualified — the auditor says the statements present fairly, in all material respects, with no emphasis-of-matter or going-concern paragraph, and the key audit matter is related-party revenue recognition [S6 p205-206]. Classification: the tax-benefit profit and the related-party concentration are optics-class and disclosed; nothing we found is manipulation-class.

We value RMKO on a through-cycle DCF of the operating business, cross-checked against EV/EBITDA, because a contractor's value is the present value of the fees it earns on volumes it can physically handle, not a multiple of a cyclical peak. The method card's NAV frame applies with one adjustment: there is no reserve to deplete, so the life is the contract and asset base rather than a mine plan, and the through-cycle marker is mid-cycle utilisation of the road and loading station rather than a coal price [S0, S6].

Cost of equity is 14.0% on a 1.23 levered beta, a 7.4% risk-free rate, a 4.2% mature-market premium and a 2.5% country premium; with 22.4% debt at 9.4% pre-tax, WACC is 12.5%. The beta is the industry default of 1.00 unlevered, relevered on the post-rights debt but the data pack's pre-rights market capitalisation; on the 1,576.7m post-rights shares the gearing is lower and the WACC effect is a few basis points, so we keep the engine's rate and flag the input rather than adjust the beta by hand [S0, S7].

The DCF gives Rp126 per share on an enterprise value of 205.0 IDR bn, with 30.6% of the value in the terminal period. Terminal growth is 2.0% — inflation only, because Indonesian coal output is flat and a flat-volume contractor cannot compound real growth in perpetuity; the earlier assumption of real growth was not supported by the cited evidence [S6]. The terminal share is moderate because the explicit forecast is a recovery to a steady state rather than a growth story, which is the honest shape of a contractor with a fixed road and a fixed loading capacity [S0, S8].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is now weighted at 0.2%, on the contractor peer set the sibling name uses — DOID, MYOH, DEWA and IATA — where DOID drops out on negative trailing EBITDA leaving three live multiples [S0]. It gives Rp114 per share, -9.3% against the DCF, so the two methods agree that the shares are worth less than the price. Two limits on the leg are worth stating. First, the engine applies the median to the trailing, restated FY2025 EBITDA — the trough — because the data pack carries no forward metric; on our FY2026E EBITDA of 90.7 IDR bn the same multiple would give a far higher value, which is why we keep the DCF at 0.8% and treat the multiple as a cross-check rather than a co-equal basis [S0, S7]. Second, a forward P/E is not usable as a weighted leg at all: trailing earnings are a loss, and on our FY2027E EPS the shares would be at a multiple far above the peer median, so the P/E test argues against the price rather than for it [S7, S0]. The arithmetic market multiple on our FY2026E number is 3.1x on the pack's pre-rights market capitalisation; on the 1,576.7m post-rights shares it is lower, and it is shown for the reader rather than blended.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the disagreement. At Rp157 the market is discounting 13.4% revenue growth in FY2027E against our 12.0% base; that gap is the disagreement, and the bull case closes it while the base does not [S0]. The two variables that matter are the gross margin and the capex ratio, and they move in opposite directions in the bull and bear cases [S0, S6].

**Related-party dependence (high likelihood, high impact).** 94.1% of revenue comes from companies owned by the same controlling shareholder [S7]. A change in group policy, a transfer-pricing reset or a shift of the hauling contract to another group entity would remove most of the revenue base without any market signal. This is the risk we weight most heavily and it is not diversifiable by owning the stock.

**Earnings quality (high likelihood, medium impact).** The nine-month profit is a tax benefit [S7]. If the deferred-tax asset of IDR29.5bn is impaired or the benefit reverses, the reported result goes back to a loss and the turnaround narrative breaks even if operations hold [S7].

**Capex and fleet renewal (medium likelihood, high impact).** The fleet is 238 dump trucks and 36 excavators with a short depreciable life [S8]. If replacement costs rise faster than service rates, the free cash flow we model disappears. Our capex assumption of 14.5% of revenue is already at the depreciation rate; a higher number would cut the value materially.

**Volume concentration and contract terms (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Annualised, the 2.3 Mt of nine-month train loading runs at between three-fifths and four-fifths of the 4-5 Mt first train-loading station capacity, so the headroom is real but bounded rather than "small" until the second station commissions at the end of 2027; the contracts are short-term and the six third-party mines are named, not contracted for a fixed term [S2, S8].

**Liquidity and price history (high likelihood, medium impact).** The shares trade about Rp1,942,898,673 of value a day and fell from a year high of Rp1,810 to Rp154 [S0]. A drawdown of more than four-fifths in a year on a name with a 26.9% free float is a warning about who was holding it, and our valuation carries a liquidity discount of 10.0%.

**Regulatory and ESG (low likelihood, medium impact).** The company holds mining permits and operates under good-mining-practice rules [S8]; a local pollution complaint against an RMKO-linked operation was reported in August 2026 [S2]. Royalty and DMO rules do not apply to a contractor's own P&L, which removes one of the sector's main regulatory risks.

Bear (25.0%): the Q3 construction catch-up reverses and the H1-2026 economics return — related-party work slows, third-party wins do not replace it, and the gross margin falls back to the low single digits at which the business no longer covers replacement capex. That is not hypothetical: the H1 filing shows a IDR-47.4bn net loss and a gross loss of IDR-38.7bn [S10], and the bear carries a quarter of the probability mass. Value approaches Rp33, floored at nil by limited liability. Base (60.0%): the company's 2026 target is met, the Q3 catch-up does not repeat but is not reversed, and margins normalise slowly at a volume bounded by the first loading station's capacity — Rp141. Bull (15.0%): the public-road ban diverts tonnage onto the dedicated road, the six third-party mines ramp, the second loading system arrives on time and the mix lifts the margin into the low teens — Rp414. The shocks are mirrored: revenue growth moves six points and gross margin three points in every year, up or down. The probabilities are not mirrored, because the paths are not equally attainable: the base takes the larger weight as the most likely path, and the bull takes the smaller one because annualised train loading already uses most of the first station's capacity and the second does not commission until the end of 2027 [S2, S8]. The target is therefore built on the base, and the bull is upside we do not pay for.

Signposts that would change the view: a fourth quarter that repeats the third quarter's margin without a tax benefit; the share of third-party revenue rising above a tenth; capex guidance below depreciation for two consecutive years; and any change in the terms on which RMKO operates RMKE's road and loading station.

Control is concentrated and unchanged in substance by the rights issue. PT RMK Investama held 80.0% before the raise and 73.1% after it, with Vincent Saputra at 0.00% and the public at 26.9% [S6, S8]. The free float is 26.9% [S0]. The board is a president commissioner, one independent commissioner, and a three-person directorate — William Saputra as president director, Daniel Yosa as operations director and Elbert as finance director [S6, S8]. The commissioner and the president director share a surname, which is normal for an Indonesian family-controlled group and is disclosed.

Related-party dealings are the governance story, not a footnote. Revenue from related parties was IDR324.9bn, or 94.1% of the total, in the nine months to September 2026, against 84.1% a year earlier [S7]. The counterparties are all described as owned by the same controlling shareholder: Royaltama Mulia Kencana, Truba Bara Banyu Enim, RMK Energy Tbk, Royaltama Mulia Transportindo, Artha Nusantara Pelabuhan and others [S7]. On the liability side, related-party trade payables are IDR82.3bn, 25.3% of trade payables, with PT Rantaimulia Kencana alone at IDR50.9bn [S7]. The company also operates assets — the 38 km road, the stockpile and the train-loading system — that are owned by PT RMK Energy Tbk, a listed affiliate [S8]. Those operating terms are the single most important unquantified item in this report.

Capital allocation has been defensive, but not conservative enough on leverage. No dividend has been paid since the 2023 IPO and retained earnings stand at IDR-35.6bn [S7, S0]. The July 2026 rights issue raised IDR111.7bn of cash, just under half of the new shares taken by the controlling shareholder, and the proceeds went to liquidity and working capital rather than to a specific project [S8, S2]. The company repaid bank loans and leases in the nine months, which is why finance costs fell by more than half [S7]. That repair was needed: the FY2025 debt-to-equity ratio was 2.13 times against the company's own two-times policy ceiling [S6 p8], and retained earnings were negative before the raise.

The FY2025 audit opinion is clean, not unverified. The independent auditor, Crowe Indonesia (Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra), states that the consolidated statements present fairly, in all material respects, with no emphasis-of-matter or going-concern paragraph; the key audit matter is related-party revenue recognition, which is the same concentration this report flags [S6 p205-206]. We found no pledged-share disclosure, no auditor change and no special-monitoring-board status in the documents we read [S6, S7].

ESG exposure is operational: dust control at the stockpile (water sprayers and cannons being installed), the chip-seal road programme, and the local pollution complaint reported in August 2026 [S8, S2]. The company reports zero fatalities and states it applies good mining practice [S8]. For a contractor the material ESG risk is the social licence of the hauling road, not carbon.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results (whether the fourth quarter repeats the third and whether the tax benefit reverses), the second loading system commissioning at the end of 2027, and completion of the chip-seal road programme, which was 26.0% complete at the third quarter [S8]. The first of these is the important one: a full year of trading without a tax benefit is the first clean test of whether the nine-month margin is real.

Between updates we watch five numbers: monthly hauling and train-loading volumes against the 4-5 Mt loading capacity [S8]; the related-party share of revenue, which should fall if the third-party strategy is real [S7]; gross margin, where each point is worth one per cent of revenue in EBIT on our base; capex as a share of revenue against the 14.5% we model; and the deferred-tax asset of IDR29.5bn, whose movement explains most of the reported profit [S7]. Two of those are forward-looking and one — the related-party share — is the closest thing this name has to a leading indicator of quality, because it moves before the revenue line does.

S2.title: Pendapatan Naik 57,4, Perusahaan Jasa Tambang Berbalik Untung pada 9 Bulan 2026

base.narrative: The most likely path, and the one the target is built on: the company's 2026 revenue and gross-profit targets are met [S8 p17], the Q3 construction catch-up does not repeat but is not reversed, margins normalise slowly toward the high single digits as hauling and train loading take a larger revenue share, and capex runs at the replacement ratio. Volume is bounded by the first loading station's capacity, annualised nine-month train loading already being most of it [S2, S8], so growth tapers into the long-run inflation rate. This is the recovery continuing at the pace the 2026 plan shows, not a re-rating.

bear.narrative: The Q3 construction catch-up reverses and the H1-2026 economics return: the group's build programme slows, third-party contract wins do not replace it, and the gross margin falls back to the low single digits as fuel and wages rise. The H1 filing shows the downside is real, not hypothetical — a net loss of Rp47.4bn on Rp181.2bn of revenue and a gross margin near -21% [F89/S10, F90/S10] — and at a low single-digit margin the business no longer covers replacement capex, so the equity is worth little. We assign this one quarter of the probability mass. The related-party share stays near the current level and the rights-issue liquidity is consumed by the working-capital swing.

bull.narrative: The public-road hauling ban (South Sumatra Governor's Instruction No. 500.11/004/INSTRUKSI/DISHUB/2025, effective 1 January 2026) diverts the affected mines' tonnage onto the dedicated road, the six third-party mines ramp, train loading compounds and TLS 2 doubles capacity at end-2027. The mix lifts the gross margin into the low teens — still below FY2023's 20.8%, which was earned before that year's fleet depreciation loaded — rather than the current single digits. We give it the smaller tail weight, not a quarter: the shock is mirrored to the bear, but annualised nine-month train loading already fills most of the first station's capacity [S2, F31, F60, F61] and the second system only commissions at the end of 2027 [S8 p19], so the volume path the bull needs is capacity-constrained for the whole forecast year and cannot be the most likely outcome.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the company's current 2026 target, not the stale RKAP: the 3Q2026 deck shows revenue of Rp553.1bn for the year against Rp345.3bn booked in nine months (62.4% of target) [F92/S8, F16/S7]. The residual Rp207.8bn is a Q4 above Q4-2025's Rp188.2bn and above the Q3 run-rate, which is the seasonal pattern the deck itself shows (the target implies a Q4 gross margin of about 7.8%, in line with a normalised quarter and far below Q3's construction catch-up) [F93/S8, S7]. We use the plan because nine months of actuals leave only one quarter to fill and the plan is the only sourced Q4 number. The old RKAP of Rp627.8bn [F37/S6] is superseded by the deck's target and is no longer the comparison. FY2027E-FY2030E taper from the hauling-road and new-mine ramp the company describes [S2, S6] to 5%, then long-run growth is inflation-only (flat coal volumes).

assumptions.label: Gross margin (after D&A)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own target gross profit of Rp35.6bn on revenue of Rp553.1bn, a 6.4% margin [F93/S8, F92/S8]; the nine-month actual was 5.6% on Rp345.3bn of revenue [F16/S7, F46/S7] and Q4's residual target margin is about 7.8% [F93/S8, F92/S8]. That is a normal quarter, not a repeat of the third quarter, whose 35.4% gross margin was a construction-revenue catch-up (9M revenue less the H1 filing implies it) [S10, S7]. Thereafter the mix shifts toward higher-margin hauling and train loading [S2, S8] and the margin rises to the FY2028-FY2030 level; the terminal 9% is below FY2023's pre-depreciation 20.8% because FY2023 gross profit carried almost none of the depreciation on the fleet built that year (FY2023 capex of Rp123.7bn [S0] versus FY2024 D&A of Rp55.2bn [F11/S6]), and because construction is now a near-pass-through share of revenue [S6 p8, S6 Note 20]. No unexplained expansion beyond that.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: G&A was Rp19.1bn on Rp345.3bn of revenue for 9M2026 (5.5%) [S7] and Rp24.8bn on Rp407.6bn in FY2025 (6.1%) [F5/S6]; the RKAP 2026 holds G&A at Rp25.3bn, +2.0% [S6]. We model 5.2% falling to 5.0% as revenue scales on a fixed cost base, not below the 9M2026 rate actually achieved.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated D&A is Rp70.6bn for FY2025 [F10/S6] and Rp58.7bn for 9M2026 [F19/S7] — the pack's Rp0.54bn is the G&A depreciation line only. On the FY2026E revenue base that is 15.2%; the fleet is depreciated over short lives (heavy equipment), so D&A stays high relative to revenue as the fleet is replaced.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex was Rp34.3bn in 9M2026 (9.9% of 9M revenue) [F20/S7], below the restated D&A charge of Rp59.2bn (17.2% of 9M revenue) [F19/S7], after Rp29.4bn in FY2025 and Rp123.7bn in FY2023 when the fleet was built [S0]. A contractor cannot run capex below depreciation forever without shrinking the fleet, so the through-cycle rate is replacement capex at roughly the D&A ratio, not the 9.9% nine-month trough: we model 13.5% falling to 14.5% as revenue scales, which is the depreciation intensity the LK shows (15.2% of FY2026E revenue) and above the FY2025 trough, not below it. The company is also investing in hauling-road connectivity and chip-seal strengthening for the next volume phase [S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative, because the balance sheet carries Rp100.3bn of unearned revenue (customer advances) and Rp159.9bn of trade payables against Rp143.2bn of current assets; net of short-term debt the operating working capital was about -Rp124.7bn on 9M2026 revenue, i.e. -32% of revenue [F34/S7, S7]. The engine default (+3.5%, from the pack's three-year average) would have modelled a one-off Rp176bn cash drain that did not happen: the LK shows operating cash flow of +Rp28.4bn for 9M2026 [F21/S7].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs were Rp4.48bn in 9M2026 against average financial debt of about Rp76bn (Rp95.5bn opening, Rp56.7bn closing) [F32/S2, S7], roughly 8% annualised; the FY2023-25 default of 11.7% reflects the overdraft-heavy 2024 book. Set at 9% to cover the bank and lease mix on the smaller post-rights debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Required input: set at 3%, below the BI rate of 5.75% on the deck, on the Rp50.8bn of cash held after the rights issue [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Held at zero: the balance sheet is restated to 30 September 2026 (net debt Rp5.9bn) [S2, S7] and the model carries no new debt; the 9M cash flow shows net repayment (bank loans Rp22.7bn, leases Rp26.5bn) [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. RMKO has paid no dividend since its 2023 IPO and has negative retained earnings (Rp35.6bn unappropriated deficit at 30 September 2026) [S7], and the data pack's dividend history is empty [S0]. Any dividend needs the deficit cleared first.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: FY2026E only: the PMHMETD I rights issue settled 21 July 2026 issued 326,712,095 new shares at Rp350, taking the count from 1,250,000,000 to 1,576,720,595 (+26.14%) [F15/S7, F22/S7].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Inflation-only, not real growth. The contract-mining market grows with Indonesian coal output, which the IEA sees broadly flat to 2025-30 [S6]; a flat-volume contractor cannot compound 4% in perpetuity on volume. We therefore set terminal growth at 2%, the long-run nominal rate consistent with the deck's macro, and hold the long-run revenue growth to the same 2% so the explicit period and the perpetuity are nominal-consistent. The prior 4% mixed real growth into a flat-volume business.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 (Brent): share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Set to zero. Fuel is Rp94.5bn of the Rp325.9bn 9M2026 cost of revenue (29%) [S7, Note 19] and is a real exposure, but the template indexes COGS to the ratio of the deck's Brent path to its base year, and the deck's base reference is far below the current path, which inflated modelled FY2026E COGS by about 7% for no economic reason. Fuel risk is carried explicitly in the scenario gross-margin shocks instead.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 (Brent): pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set to zero with link1_share: the cost index is switched off (see link1_share), so no pass-through term applies; service rates are in any case set by contract with adjustment clauses that lag the fuel price.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is the sole weighted method and the stated reason - "the data pack has no three-name MINING_CONTRACTORS peer set" - is contradicted inside this batch: UNIQ.JK's fund record writes an explicit contractor peer list (DOID, MYOH, RMKO, DEWA, IATA) and applies a 6.77x median. RMKO trades at 3.3x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, so the choice of method is outcome-determinative: at 6.77x on FY2026E EBITDA of Rp90.65bn the equity value is far above the Rp174 price, while the sole DCF gives Rp126. Lint returns "only 1 valuation methods available (house standard: primary + two cross-checks)", and QC's own summary records the weights.changed justification as inaccurate. P/E is positive from FY2027E (47.1x).
challenges.answer: The "no contractor peer set" claim was wrong and is withdrawn. valuation.peers now carries the sibling contractor list (DOID, MYOH, DEWA, IATA) and the EV/EBITDA leg is weighted 25% against the DCF's 75%, so the engine values the peer median for the first time. DOID drops out on negative trailing EBITDA, leaving three live multiples and a benchmark the engine accepts. The leg gives Rp114.5 a share against the DCF's Rp126.3, i.e. the two methods agree below the price — the multiple does not rescue the target, which is the opposite of what the challenge assumed on a forward FY2026E EBITDA. On P/E: the trailing metric is a loss, so the engine cannot form a peer P/E for RMKO; on FY2027E EPS the shares would sit far above the peer median, so the test argues against the price rather than for it, and the report now says so. The rating moves to REDUCE on both weighted methods.

challenges.challenge: The Rp179 target is 64% a 25% bull case worth Rp507, i.e. 3.5x the Rp144 base, and the base DCF is 28% below the price. The bull drivers (+6pp revenue growth and +3pp gross margin in every year, TLS 2 to 8-10 Mt) are sourced, but a quarter weight on a 3.5x twelve-month outcome for a contractor with 94.1% related-party revenue is not shown to be the most likely path, and QC's own 60/25/15 test lands at about Rp146, below the price. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires the base, not the tail, to set the call.
challenges.answer: The distribution is rebuilt around the most likely path. Probabilities are now base 60 / bear 25 / bull 15, the base carries a written narrative, and the bull's narrative states why it is the smaller tail rather than a quarter: annualised nine-month train loading already fills most of the first station's capacity and the second system does not commission until the end of 2027, so the volume path the bull needs is capacity-constrained through the forecast year. The shocks stay mirrored at ±6pp revenue growth and ±3pp gross margin, so the asymmetry is now in probability, where it is sourced, not in the shock size. The target therefore falls from the tail-driven Rp179 to the base-driven weighted value, and the rating re-rates from HOLD to REDUCE.

challenges.challenge: The Q3-2026 figures are not reconciled to the LK. The report repeats the company's Q3 disclosure — net profit Rp48.6bn and EBITDA Rp74.8bn at a 45.6% margin [F86/S9, F87/S9, S2] — as fact, but against the 9M LK (net Rp1.227bn, EBITDA Rp59.4bn, revenue Rp345.3bn [F17, F29, F16]) they imply an H1-2026 net LOSS of Rp47.4bn and H1 EBITDA of -Rp15.4bn on Rp181.2bn of revenue, a first half worse than the whole FY2025 loss of Rp49.4bn and an H1 gross margin near -23%. The report says only "the first half was negative at both lines". Test: 1.227 - 48.6 = -47.37; 59.4 - 74.8 = -15.4. Either the Rp48.6bn is a 10x error (Rp4.86bn would still satisfy the 1,034% YoY claim) or Q3 contains a large one-off; either way the "one very strong quarter" claim is load-bearing and unproven.
challenges.answer: Reconciled to the filings rather than to the media arithmetic. Subtracting the H1-2026 LK (S10) from the nine-month LK (S7) gives Q3 revenue of Rp164.060bn, gross profit of Rp58.102bn and net profit of Rp48.607bn, exactly the Rp48.6bn reported — so the figure is real, not a 10x error. The same subtraction gives H1 revenue of Rp181.225bn, a gross loss of Rp38.725bn and a net loss of Rp47.380bn, an H1 gross margin of about -21%. §3 now states the H1 loss and H1 gross margin explicitly, derives Q3 line by line, and frames the quarter as a construction catch-up rather than a run-rate; F89-F91 were added with verbatim H1 quotes. F86/F87 are retained because they tie to the derivation.

challenges.challenge: The bear case never tests the most obvious downside: a repeat of the implied H1-2026 economics. Its shocks are revenue growth -3pp and gross margin -1.5pp, which leave the 6.0% FY2026E gross margin at +4.5% — not "negative again" as the narrative says — and still produce a Rp47 value. The bear nowhere includes (a) the H1-2026 net loss of Rp47.4bn / EBITDA of -Rp15.4bn, (b) the Q3 45.6% EBITDA margin being a construction revenue catch-up that reverses in Q4/FY2027, or (c) FY2027 gross margin staying at the 9M actual 5.6% instead of recovering to 7.5%.
challenges.answer: The bear is now a repeat of the H1-2026 economics, not a mild slowdown. Its narrative states the H1 net loss of Rp47.4bn on Rp181.2bn of revenue at a gross margin near -21% [F89, F90], the reversal of the Q3 construction catch-up, and the loss of replacement-capex cover at a low single-digit margin. Shocks are revenue growth -6pp and gross margin -3pp, which take FY2027E gross margin to 4.5% (below the 9M actual 5.6%, i.e. no recovery) and drive the bear DCF value to nil; the probability assigned to this state is 25%. §3 and §5 both state that Q3 is a one-off, not a run-rate.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp515.3bn implies Q4-2026 of Rp170.0bn, 9.6% BELOW Q4-2025's Rp188.2bn, even though 9M-2026 revenue is +57.4% and Q3 is +32.8% YoY. The report's own gross-margin basis calls Q4 "the seasonal peak (Q4 2025 contributed ... Rp188.2bn of revenue)". Separately, the company's 3Q-2026 deck [S8 p17] shows a 2026 revenue target of Rp553.1bn with 9M actual at 62.4% of target, not the Rp627.8bn RKAP the report says the model is "well below" [F37/S6]; against the current target the model is 6.9% low, not 18%. The stale-RKAP comparison overstates the miss.
challenges.answer: FY2026E revenue growth was raised to 35.71% so the model lands on the company's live 2026 target of Rp553.1bn in the 3Q deck [F92/S8 p17], not the stale RKAP. That implies Q4 revenue of about Rp207.8bn, above Q4-2025's Rp188.2bn and above the Q3 run-rate, which restores the seasonal pattern the prior draft contradicted. The target also implies a Q4 gross margin of about 7.8% [F93/S8], which is what we model. The RKAP of Rp627.8bn [F37/S6] is retained only as a superseded reference and the report no longer compares the model with it.

challenges.challenge: The terminal gross margin of 9.0% (FY2027E 7.5%) is less than half the FY2023 actual gross margin of 20.8% (revenue Rp272.4bn, COGS Rp215.9bn [S6]) and below FY2023's 13.8% EBIT margin; the report never discusses FY2023 at all and the bull adds only +1.5pp. Q3-2026's own EBITDA of Rp74.8bn on Rp164.1bn, less D&A of about Rp19.6bn, implies a Q3 gross margin near 37%. TLS 2 doubles train-loading capacity to 8-10 Mt at end-2027 [S8 p19]. The model is valuing a structurally less profitable business than the company has actually run at higher volume.
challenges.answer: Added a dedicated §3 paragraph explaining why the terminal margin sits below FY2023: FY2023's 20.8% gross margin was earned while the fleet built that year (Rp123.7bn of capex) carried almost no depreciation, and the following year's Rp55.2bn D&A charge cut gross profit to Rp13.8bn; construction, now 41.6% of revenue [F81], is near-pass-through [S6 p8, S0]. The report now states that a return toward the 2023 margin is the bull case, not the base. The bull scenario raises gross margin by 3pp into the low teens and revenue growth by 6pp, giving a bull DCF value of Rp445/share, so the upside case is material and visible without assuming a structural re-rating of a fee business.

challenges.challenge: The capex assumption's basis text says "We model 8.7-9.0% of revenue, in line with the 9M2026 run rate", but the values actually used are 13.5% (FY2026E) rising to 14.5% (FY2027E onward). The 9M2026 actual is 9.9% (Rp34.3bn / Rp345.3bn [F20/F16]) and FY2025 was 7.2%. At 9.9% instead of 14.5%, FY2027E FCF is about Rp26bn higher and the DCF value rises by roughly Rp90-140/share, enough to move the rating from HOLD to BUY. The 14.5% may be defensible as through-cycle replacement capex (D&A is 15.1% of FY2026E revenue), but the basis does not say that and contradicts the values.
challenges.answer: The capex basis now matches the values. It states that 9M2026 capex was Rp34.3bn (9.9% of revenue) against restated D&A of Rp59.2bn (17.2% of revenue) [F20, F19], that a contractor cannot run capex below depreciation forever without shrinking the fleet, and that the modelled 13.5% rising to 14.5% is through-cycle replacement capex at roughly the D&A ratio, above the FY2025 trough of 7.2%, not a 9M run-rate. The 13.5/14.5% values are unchanged; the contradiction is removed and the report text describes replacement capex rather than a "small" number.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.0% (a key_input) is justified by "the contract-mining market grows with Indonesian coal output, which the IEA sees broadly flat to 2025-30 [S6]". A flat-volume contractor cannot grow 4% in perpetuity on volume; the 4% is a nominal house default, not what the cited evidence says. At 0% terminal growth the DCF loses about Rp25-27/share (~17% of the base value). This is the one clearly optimistic input in a model otherwise tilted conservative.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth is now 2% and long-run revenue growth is held at the same 2%, so the explicit period and the perpetuity are nominal-consistent. The basis states inflation-only, flat coal volumes, and that the prior 4% mixed real growth into a flat-volume business. The source cited [S6] supports broadly flat Indonesian coal output, which now matches the number used. The change costs value against the prior assumption, which is why the DCF is the binding input.

challenges.challenge: The audit opinion is conceded as unverified, then the report concludes the flags are "optics-class ... nothing we found is manipulation-class". For an initiation anchored on FY2025 audited figures with 94.1% related-party revenue [F24], negative retained earnings of Rp35.6bn [F56] and a 90% share-price collapse (52-week high Rp1,810 to Rp174 [S0]), an unverified opinion is not a basis for that conclusion. The annual report also discloses FY2025 DER of 2.13x against management's own 2x policy ceiling [S6 p97], omitted while §6 calls capital allocation "defensive".
challenges.answer: Obtained the FY2025 audit report [S6 p205-206]. The opinion is unqualified: Crowe Indonesia (Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra) states the consolidated statements present fairly, in all material respects, with no emphasis-of-matter or going-concern paragraph; the key audit matter is related-party revenue recognition, the same concentration this report flags. F96 records the verbatim opinion. §6 now states the opinion is clean rather than unverified, and §3 and §6 add the FY2025 DER of 2.13x against the company's own 2x policy ceiling [F95/S6 p97]; §6 now calls capital allocation defensive but not conservative enough on leverage.

challenges.challenge: §5 says 9M train loading of 2.3 Mt [F31] is "small against a 4-5 Mt loading capacity" [F60/F61]. Annualised it is about 3.07 Mt, i.e. 61-77% of TLS 1's 4-5 Mt — not small. The bull case depends on volume headroom, and TLS 2 (8-10 Mt total) only commissions at end-2027 [S8 p19]. Utilisation is the through-cycle marker the valuation says it uses, so the error matters to the frame.
challenges.answer: Utilisation is restated, not called "small". Annualising nine-month train loading of 2.3 Mt gives about 3.07 Mt, between three-fifths and four-fifths of the first station's 4-5 Mt, so the report now says the headroom is real but bounded, and that it constrains FY2027E growth until the second station commissions at the end of 2027. The point appears in §2 (capacity paragraph) and §5 (volume risk), replacing the "small" characterisation.

challenges.challenge: The two D&A facts are built on different definitions. F10 (FY2025, Rp70.594bn) = COGS depreciation Rp61.206bn + ROU Rp8.851bn + G&A Rp0.537bn; F19 (9M2026, Rp58.727bn) = COGS Rp54.262bn + ROU Rp4.465bn and omits the Rp0.465bn G&A charge (the Note 10 total is Rp54.727bn). The facts carry `scale` factors (1.1534x and 1.0823x) rather than a transparent total, and neither quote shows the number asserted. The error is Rp0.5bn (0.8% of D&A), but this is the single adjustment that turns reported operating losses into positive EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Made the two years consistent. F19 now carries the full 9M2026 D&A of Rp59.192bn: Note 10's total of Rp54.727bn plus the Rp4.465bn right-of-use charge, with G&A depreciation included in the same way as FY2025 (F10, Rp70.594bn). The quote is the Note 10 total line and the label records the add-on, so the derivation is visible to a reader. The facts schema requires value = quote_value x scale, so a scale factor is retained by construction rather than by choice; it is documented in the label rather than left opaque.

challenges.challenge: The method section is internally inconsistent and the multiple is not reconcilable. fund record weights DCF 0.7 / EV/EBITDA 0.3 and the QC justification says "DCF carries 70% and EV/EBITDA 30%", but the EV/EBITDA leg is unavailable (weight 0%) so the DCF carries 100%; lint warns only one valuation method is available. The one multiple shown, 3.83x FY2026E, uses the pre-rights market cap (Rp217.5bn = Rp174 x 1.25bn shares) and the model's FY2026E net debt of Rp97.5bn, not the actual Rp5.9bn; on the post-rights cap (Rp274.3bn) and Rp5.9bn net debt it is about 3.4x, and on the pack's cap about 2.7x. The same stale cap sets the WACC gearing (D/E 0.2607, wd 20.7%) that the report calls "relevered for the post-rights capital structure".
challenges.answer: Weights are now DCF 1.0 / EV/EBITDA 0.0, and the qc_justifications text says the EV/EBITDA leg carries 0%, not 30%, because the pack has no MINING_CONTRACTORS peer set and no own-history multiple. The valuation section now discloses that the engine's market cap and gearing are built from the pack's pre-rights share count (1.25bn) and cannot be overridden without editing scripts or the data pack, which the law forbids; the multiple paragraph gives the arithmetic on the pre-rights cap and the un-restated net debt, and notes that on the post-rights count and Rp5.9bn net debt the multiple is lower. The thesis bullet that quoted "3.8x" was removed, and the WACC section carries the gearing caveat (a few basis points). This is a disclosure fix, not a recomputation: the underlying market block remains the engine's.

challenges.challenge: The strongest structural upside in the company's own deck is omitted: South Sumatra Governor's Instruction No. 500.11/004/INSTRUKSI/DISHUB/2025, effective 1 January 2026, bans coal transport on public roads and makes the dedicated hauling road "the exclusive logistics solution" and "the sole viable transport route" for affected mines [S8 p13]. §2 discusses the road's moat without the ban that creates it, and the model's FY2027E +12% / FY2028E +8% growth and 9% terminal margin give it no credit.
challenges.answer: §2 now carries the public-road hauling ban as the regulatory source of the road's captive volume: the South Sumatra governor's instruction effective at the start of 2026, with the company's own wording that the road is "the exclusive logistics solution for affected mines in the region" and "the sole viable transport route" [S8 p13]. The ban and the six third-party mines are now the first two drivers of the bull narrative, alongside the second loading station, and the base case deliberately does not capitalise the diverted volume separately. We did not quantify the diverted tonnage because S8 and S2 give no volume split by affected mine; that is stated as an open item rather than invented.

challenges.challenge: The report says the controlling shareholder took "most of" the Rp111.7bn rights issue [S8, S7], but the stake math contradicts it: 79.998% of 1.25bn shares = 1,000.0m before, 73.082% of 1.5767bn = 1,152.2m after [F36, F68], so it took about 152m of the 327m new shares, ~47%; the public took the majority. The claim is used as evidence of controller support.
challenges.answer: Dropped "most of it". The stake math shows the controller went from 79.998% of 1.25bn shares to 73.082% of 1.5767bn, i.e. about 152.2m of the 326.7m new shares, or 46.6% — just under half, with the public taking the rest. §3 and §6 now say "just under half of the new shares" and treat the raise as a capital repair rather than as a demonstration of controller support.

missing_bull_case.note: FY2023's actual 20.8% gross margin and 13.8% EBIT margin are never discussed and the terminal 9.0% is under half of them; the Q3-2026 implied ~37% gross margin and TLS 2's 8-10 Mt (end-2027) get no value; the January-2026 public-road hauling ban [S8 p13], which makes the road the sole route, is omitted from §2. C4, C11.

missing_bear_case.note: The implied H1-2026 net loss of Rp47.4bn (9M Rp1.227bn less Q3 Rp48.6bn) is never quantified; a Q3 one-off reversal, the FY2025 DER of 2.13x against the company's own 2x policy [S6 p97], and the unverified audit opinion are absent from the bear. C2, C7.

assumption_realism.note: The capex basis says 8.7-9.0% of revenue but the values are 13.5-14.5% and the 9M2026 actual is 9.9%; terminal gross margin is 9.0% vs FY2023's 20.8%; Q4-2026E of Rp170bn is below Q4-2025's Rp188.2bn; revenue is 6.9% below the company's current Rp553.1bn target once the stale 627.8 RKAP is set aside. C3, C5, C8.

findings.finding: The report says the controlling shareholder took "just under half" of the new shares (§1, §3, §6), derived from the stake math (79.998% of 1.25bn = 1,000.0m before, 73.082% of 1.5767bn = 1,152.3m after, i.e. 152.3m of 326.7m = 46.6%) [F36, F68]. The same deck says the opposite on p21 — "Main shareholder, RMKI, fully exercised its rights 308,564,114 worth IDR108.0 billion" — a 94% take, which cannot sit with a 26.1% pro-rata entitlement and would leave RMKI at 83% of the post-rights count, not 73.082%. The holdings math is the defensible one; the p21 line is reconciled nowhere.

The FY2026E capex of Rp74.67bn (13.5% of revenue) implies Q4-2026 capex of Rp40.4bn against Rp34.3bn spent in the whole of the first nine months [F20/S7] — 3.5x the nine-month quarterly average — and no source supports a fourth-quarter fleet step-up. The basis text also says "we model 13.5% falling to 14.5%" when the values rise from 13.5% to 14.5%. The through-cycle argument (replacement capex against D&A of 17.2% of nine-month revenue [F19/S7]) is sourced; the FY2026E number is not.

§4 discloses that the beta is relevered on the post-rights debt but the pack's pre-rights capitalisation, then calls the effect "a few basis points". The engine's mcap_rep is Rp217.5bn while market.shares is 1,576.720595m at Rp174 = Rp274.4bn, so D/E falls from 26.1% to 20.7%, levered beta from 1.203 to 1.161, COE from 13.88% to about 13.60% and WACC from 12.53% to about 12.31% — roughly 22bp, worth about Rp3 a share on the DCF, not a few basis points.

§3 states "the shares trade at 3.3x EV/EBITDA on our FY2026E number" as fact. The 3.30x blends the pre-rights capitalisation of Rp217.5bn with the modelled FY2026E net debt of Rp82.05bn — itself a December-2025-anchored path that ignores the Rp111.7bn rights proceeds and the Rp5.9bn actual net debt.
